## How do I access Airline On-Time Statistics?

## Answer

### Sources of Airline On-Time Statistics

### There are several ways to access statistics on on-time performance, delays, and cancelations.

* * *

### Prepared Tables

*   [Airline On-Time Statistics Press Releases](http://www.bts.dot.gov/statistical-releases?field_effective_date_value=&field_effective_date_value_1=&combine=&field_editorial_type_target_id=366)

*   [Air Travel Consumer Reports by carrier and airport (including mishandled-baggage statistics)](http://www.transportation.gov/airconsumer/air-travel-consumer-reports)

*   [Airline On-Time data tables (arrival and departure performance rankings)](http://www.bts.gov/topics/airline-time-tables)

* * *

### Simple Searches

*   [On-Time Performance - Flight Delays at a Glance by year and month](http://www.transtats.bts.gov/HomeDrillChart.asp)

*   [Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes](http://www.transtats.bts.gov/OT_Delay/OT_DelayCause1.asp)

* * *

### Detailed Statistics

Access detailed data on [the TranStats platform:](http://www.transtats.bts.gov/)

On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases

[![Image 2: Select "Aviation"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-1.jpg)](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-1.jpg)

Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"

[![Image 3: Select "Airline On-Time Performance Data"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-2.jpg)](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-2.jpg)

Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.

![Image 4: Marketing Carrier and Reporting Carrier](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/276824/images/MarketingvsReporting.PNG)

To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.

Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:

![Image 5: Select "Analysis"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-4.jpg)

To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years

![Image 6: Select "Crosstabs"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-5.jpg)

**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field

![Image 7: Select "Unique Carrier" for AirlineID](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-6.jpg)

To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"

![Image 8: Select "Download results"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-7.jpg)

To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)

![Image 9: Select "Search the Results"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-8.jpg)

* * *

### Download Bulk Data

Accessthe raw data in TranStats:

*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time

On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases

[![Image 10: Select "Aviation"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-1.jpg)](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-1.jpg)

Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"

[![Image 11: Select "Airline On-Time Performance Data"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-2.jpg)](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-2.jpg)

To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:

![Image 12](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/276824/images/MarketingvsReporting2.png)

*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want. 
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.

![Image 13: Limit search results with "Filter Geography", "Filter Year", "Filter Period", and "Field Names"](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-10.jpg)

Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:

![Image 14: Select "Download" after filtering data](https://libapps.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/137076/images/TranStats-11.jpg)

* * *

### Other Resources

*   ### [14 CFR 234](https://www.ecfr.gov/cgi-bin/text-idx?SID=a9aed74b89913431808b3e9be0e0c3e1&mc=true&node=pt14.4.234&rgn=div5)- reporting requirements

*   [Accounting and Reporting Directives](https://www.bts.gov/topics/airlines-and-airports/accounting-and-reporting-directives): Scroll down under "AIRLINE SERVICE QUALITY PERFORMANCE" to see which carriers file on-time data in a particular year, how it's done, and what is included in the data.

## Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes (BTS)

[Data Card](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/daryaheyko/airline-on-time-statistics-and-delay-causes-bts/data)[Code (0)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/daryaheyko/airline-on-time-statistics-and-delay-causes-bts/code)[Discussion (0)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/daryaheyko/airline-on-time-statistics-and-delay-causes-bts/discussion)[Suggestions (0)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/daryaheyko/airline-on-time-statistics-and-delay-causes-bts/suggestions)

## About Dataset

This raw dataset was pulled from the Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes dashboard on the Bureau of Transportation Statistics website with a date range of June 2003 to January 2025 for all carriers and all airports.

A flight is considered delayed when it arrived 15 or more minutes than the schedule. Delayed minutes are calculated for delayed flights only.  
 When multiple causes are assigned to one delayed flight, each cause is prorated based on delayed minutes it is responsible for. The displayed numbers are rounded and may not add up to the total.

Source: [https://transtats.bts.gov/OT_Delay/OT_DelayCause1.asp](https://transtats.bts.gov/OT_Delay/OT_DelayCause1.asp) (Bureau of Transportation Statistics, Airline Service Quality Performance 234)

## About Dataset

This raw dataset was pulled from the Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes dashboard on the Bureau of Transportation Statistics website with a date range of June 2003 to January 2025 for all carriers and all airports.

A flight is considered delayed when it arrived 15 or more minutes than the schedule. Delayed minutes are calculated for delayed flights only.  
 When multiple causes are assigned to one delayed flight, each cause is prorated based on delayed minutes it is responsible for. The displayed numbers are rounded and may not add up to the total.

Source: [https://transtats.bts.gov/OT_Delay/OT_DelayCause1.asp](https://transtats.bts.gov/OT_Delay/OT_DelayCause1.asp) (Bureau of Transportation Statistics, Airline Service Quality Performance 234)

## Airline On-Time Statistics

**NOTE: Data are available from January 1995 through **June 2026**. Times are reported in local time using a 24 hour clock.**  
**Reporting changes due to mergers.** Joint reporting begins after Federal Aviation Administration approval of a single operating certificate.

*    Jan. 2006: **US Airways (US)** and **America West (HP)** start to report jointly as **US Airways (US)**. 
*    Jan. 2010: **Delta (DL)** and **Northwest (NW)** start to report jointly as **Delta (DL)**. 
*    Jan. 2012: **United (UA)** and **Continental (CO)** start to report jointly as **United (UA)**. 
*    Jan. 2012: **Atlantic Southeast (EV)** and **ExpressJet (XE)** start to report jointly as **ExpressJet (EV)**, presented here as **ExpressJet Combined (E*)**.   
 For data through Dec. 31, 2011, use the code **EV** for **Atlantic Southeast** and the code **XE** for **ExpressJet**.   
 Beginning with January 1, 2012 data, use the code **E*** for **ExpressJet Combined**. Searches for EV or XE will find data for the period ending Dec. 31, 2011 only. Searches for E* will find data for the period beginning Jan. 1, 2012 only. 
*    Aug. 2013: **Pinnacle (9E)** changed name to **Endeavor**. 
*    Apr. 2014: **American Eagle (MQ)** changed name to **Envoy**. 
*    Jan. 2015: **Southwest (WN)** and **AirTran (FL)** start to report jointly as **Southwest (WN)**. 
*    Jul. 2015: **American (AA)** and **US Airways (US)** start to report jointly as **American (AA)**. 
*    Apr. 2018: **Alaska (AS) and Virgin America (VX) start to report jointly as Alaska (AS)**.

Airline on-time data are reported in 2021 to the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) by the 17 U.S.[air carriers](https://www.bts.dot.gov/explore-topics-and-geography/topics/airline-time-performance-and-causes-flight-delays) that have at least 0.5 percent of total domestic scheduled-service passenger revenues.

## Airline On-Time Statistics

**NOTE: Data are available from January 1995 through **June 2026**. Times are reported in local time using a 24 hour clock.**  
**Reporting changes due to mergers.** Joint reporting begins after Federal Aviation Administration approval of a single operating certificate.

*    Jan. 2006: **US Airways (US)** and **America West (HP)** start to report jointly as **US Airways (US)**. 
*    Jan. 2010: **Delta (DL)** and **Northwest (NW)** start to report jointly as **Delta (DL)**. 
*    Jan. 2012: **United (UA)** and **Continental (CO)** start to report jointly as **United (UA)**. 
*    Jan. 2012: **Atlantic Southeast (EV)** and **ExpressJet (XE)** start to report jointly as **ExpressJet (EV)**, presented here as **ExpressJet Combined (E*)**.   
 For data through Dec. 31, 2011, use the code **EV** for **Atlantic Southeast** and the code **XE** for **ExpressJet**.   
 Beginning with January 1, 2012 data, use the code **E*** for **ExpressJet Combined**. Searches for EV or XE will find data for the period ending Dec. 31, 2011 only. Searches for E* will find data for the period beginning Jan. 1, 2012 only. 
*    Aug. 2013: **Pinnacle (9E)** changed name to **Endeavor**. 
*    Apr. 2014: **American Eagle (MQ)** changed name to **Envoy**. 
*    Jan. 2015: **Southwest (WN)** and **AirTran (FL)** start to report jointly as **Southwest (WN)**. 
*    Jul. 2015: **American (AA)** and **US Airways (US)** start to report jointly as **American (AA)**. 
*    Apr. 2018: **Alaska (AS) and Virgin America (VX) start to report jointly as Alaska (AS)**.

**WASHINGTON —**
About 6 million U.S. travelers are expected to fly domestically this Thanksgiving holiday, with Orlando, San Francisco and Honolulu among the top destinations, according to [AAA](https://newsroom.aaa.com/2025/11/aaa-thanksgiving-travel-forecast-2025/).

Travelers heading to Honolulu are in luck, Daniel K. Inouye International Airport had the best on-time performance in 2025 among the top 50 U.S. airports by passenger traffic, according to the [Bureau of Transportation Statistics](https://www.transtats.bts.gov/airports.asp).

Advertisement

Honolulu's airport saw 87% of arrivals and 88% of departures leave on time from August 2024 to July 2025. That is based on the most recent data BTS provides for domestic flights and labels the period as 2025 data. From this time period, Daniel K. Inouye had a total of 25,300 flights.

Salt Lake City International, St. Louis Lambert International and John Wayne Airport-Orange County had the next highest on-time arrival rates, each at 85%. Among the three, Salt Lake City had the most domestic flights with 115,000, while St. Louis Lambert and John Wayne had a combined 45,800.

The lowest on-time arrival rates were at Ronald Reagan Washington National and Newark Liberty International, with both at 72%. Between August 2024 and July 2025, Reagan operated 141,800 flights and Newark operated 122,600. Philadelphia International had the second-lowest on-time arrival rate at 74% with 99,600 flights.

Three airports were behind Honolulu for on-time departures: Portland International, Kansas City International and Indianapolis International. All had an on-time departure rate of 86%.

Dallas-Fort Worth International had the lowest on-time departure rate of 71% with 318,100 flights.

Baltimore Washington International Thurgood Marshall had a slightly higher on-time departure rate of 73%, but far fewer flights — 97,000 compared to Dallas-Fort Worth.

Still, Dallas-Fort Worth was not the busiest airport in the country. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International had 326,600 flights, with an on-time departure rate of 77% and 81% for arrivals.

**WASHINGTON —**
About 6 million U.S. travelers are expected to fly domestically this Thanksgiving holiday, with Orlando, San Francisco and Honolulu among the top destinations, according to [AAA](https://newsroom.aaa.com/2025/11/aaa-thanksgiving-travel-forecast-2025/).

Travelers heading to Honolulu are in luck, Daniel K. Inouye International Airport had the best on-time performance in 2025 among the top 50 U.S. airports by passenger traffic, according to the [Bureau of Transportation Statistics](https://www.transtats.bts.gov/airports.asp).

Advertisement

Honolulu's airport saw 87% of arrivals and 88% of departures leave on time from August 2024 to July 2025. That is based on the most recent data BTS provides for domestic flights and labels the period as 2025 data. From this time period, Daniel K. Inouye had a total of 25,300 flights.

Salt Lake City International, St. Louis Lambert International and John Wayne Airport-Orange County had the next highest on-time arrival rates, each at 85%. Among the three, Salt Lake City had the most domestic flights with 115,000, while St. Louis Lambert and John Wayne had a combined 45,800.

The lowest on-time arrival rates were at Ronald Reagan Washington National and Newark Liberty International, with both at 72%. Between August 2024 and July 2025, Reagan operated 141,800 flights and Newark operated 122,600. Philadelphia International had the second-lowest on-time arrival rate at 74% with 99,600 flights.

Three airports were behind Honolulu for on-time departures: Portland International, Kansas City International and Indianapolis International. All had an on-time departure rate of 86%.

Dallas-Fort Worth International had the lowest on-time departure rate of 71% with 318,100 flights.

Baltimore Washington International Thurgood Marshall had a slightly higher on-time departure rate of 73%, but far fewer flights — 97,000 compared to Dallas-Fort Worth.

Still, Dallas-Fort Worth was not the busiest airport in the country. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International had 326,600 flights, with an on-time departure rate of 77% and 81% for arrivals.

#### What is OTP

On-time performance (OTP) data is critical to understanding the performance of airlines and airports.

Across the aviation industry, an airline departure or arrival occurring****within 15 minutes****of the scheduled time is considered on-time.[](https://www.oag.com/on-time-performance-airlines-airports)

OTP is a crucial key performance indicator for airlines and airports, it helps to gauge their efficiency and also has the potential to set them apart from their competitors.

#### Understanding the data

On-time performance data shows the percentage of flights that have**departed (for airports)**or**arrived (for airlines)**on-time.

A flight is considered on-time if it has departed or arrived**within 15 minutes**of the schedule.

The higher the percentage, the better the OTP score.

**Cancellations**are included in our data and are considered**not**on-time.

For an airline or airport's OTP to be published, OAG requires access to flight status data for at least**80% of all scheduled flights operated,**and**to be ranked they must operate a minimum of 1,500 flights**that month.

**Not included? Contact us and we will be happy to discuss our requirements.**

[Get in touch](https://www.oag.com/airline-partner-hub)

## Frequently asked questions

*   How is airport OTP calculatedAirport on-time performance is based on actual gate departure times. Flights that depart within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Departing 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered not on-time.  
*   How is airline OTP calculated?**Airline**on-time performance is based on**actual gate****arrival times**. Flights that arrive within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Arriving 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered**not on-time**.  
*   Why is OTP important?OTP is valuable for operations management; delays affect productivity and lead to increased costs. Flight punctuality is also of the highest importance to the traveler, poor punctuality will mean that flights arrive at their gate late or depart late – which could lead to passengers missing connecting flights.   
*   Which airports are included?Airports included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 departures in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Which airlines are included?Airlines included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 scheduled flights in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Why is my airline/airport not included?To be included in OAG's rankings airlines and airports must reach a minimum size criteria and a coverage qualification. To discuss our requirements in more detail, click the link below.  
*   How often is the data refreshed?The OTP data is updated each month, usually during the second week. You can sign up to receive notifications by clicking on the link below.

#### What is OTP

On-time performance (OTP) data is critical to understanding the performance of airlines and airports.

Across the aviation industry, an airline departure or arrival occurring****within 15 minutes****of the scheduled time is considered on-time.[](https://www.oag.com/on-time-performance-airlines-airports)

OTP is a crucial key performance indicator for airlines and airports, it helps to gauge their efficiency and also has the potential to set them apart from their competitors.

#### Understanding the data

On-time performance data shows the percentage of flights that have**departed (for airports)**or**arrived (for airlines)**on-time.

A flight is considered on-time if it has departed or arrived**within 15 minutes**of the schedule.

The higher the percentage, the better the OTP score.

**Cancellations**are included in our data and are considered**not**on-time.

For an airline or airport's OTP to be published, OAG requires access to flight status data for at least**80% of all scheduled flights operated,**and**to be ranked they must operate a minimum of 1,500 flights**that month.

**Not included? Contact us and we will be happy to discuss our requirements.**

## Frequently asked questions

*   How is airport OTP calculatedAirport on-time performance is based on actual gate departure times. Flights that depart within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Departing 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered not on-time.  
*   How is airline OTP calculated?**Airline**on-time performance is based on**actual gate****arrival times**. Flights that arrive within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Arriving 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered**not on-time**.  
*   Why is OTP important?OTP is valuable for operations management; delays affect productivity and lead to increased costs. Flight punctuality is also of the highest importance to the traveler, poor punctuality will mean that flights arrive at their gate late or depart late – which could lead to passengers missing connecting flights.   
*   Which airports are included?Airports included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 departures in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Which airlines are included?Airlines included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 scheduled flights in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Why is my airline/airport not included?To be included in OAG's rankings airlines and airports must reach a minimum size criteria and a coverage qualification. To discuss our requirements in more detail, click the link below.

Global flight cancellations declined from **71,840 in July to 59,785 in August**, representing a **17% month-over-month improvement** in global aviation operations. Asia Pacific recorded the strongest reduction at **23%**, followed by North America at **20%** and the Middle East and Africa at **15%**.

**Aeromexico** became the global and Latin American leader with an **89.74% on-time arrival rate**, while **Singapore Airlines** moved into first place in Asia Pacific at **87.91%**. **WestJet, SAS and FlySafair** retained their respective regional leadership positions.

Matt — Founder September 9, 2026 7 min read

 Share

Not all airports are equal. The difference between flying through Salt Lake City and flying through Fort Lauderdale is not just geography — it is 24 percentage points of delay probability on every trip.

This ranking uses DelayGuard's dataset of 1.35 million validated US domestic flight records (BTS TranStats, 2023–2025 average) to rank 22 major US airports by the percentage of flights delayed 15 minutes or more.

## What Makes an Airport Delay-Prone?

Four factors explain most of the variation in this ranking.

### 1. Hub concentration

Airports with multiple competing hubs — ORD (United + American), DEN (United + Southwest + Frontier), JFK (Delta + JetBlue + American) — see compounding cascade delays. When United's morning bank at ORD runs late, it reduces the airspace available for American's simultaneous bank.

Airports with a single dominant hub — [ATL](https://www.delayguard.ai/airports/atl) (Delta), [SLC](https://www.delayguard.ai/airports/slc) (Delta), [SEA](https://www.delayguard.ai/airports/sea) (Alaska) — allow one airline to control the entire operation, enabling faster recovery.

### 2. Airspace congestion

The New York TRACON manages EWR, JFK, LGA, and several smaller airports simultaneously. Any disruption at any one of them constrains what the others can do. This is the structural reason all three New York airports rank in the top tier for delays — the problem is not the airports individually, it is the shared airspace above them.

### 3. Weather exposure

*   **Summer thunderstorms:** Denver, Chicago, Dallas, and the entire Northeast corridor face convective weather in June–August.
*   **Winter storms:** Boston, Minneapolis, Philadelphia, and Detroit face nor'easters, ice events, and blizzards that can close airports entirely.
*   **Fog:** San Francisco's marine layer predictably cuts runway capacity by 30–40% on summer evenings.
*   **Favorable weather:** Phoenix and Las Vegas rarely face severe weather — a structural advantage that puts them near the bottom of the delay ranking.

### 4. Slot controls

[LaGuardia](https://www.delayguard.ai/airports/lga) is the only major US commercial airport that remains fully slot-controlled for domestic operations. The FAA caps hourly arrivals and departures. This eliminates scheduling slack — any disruption has no buffer to absorb into. Despite being the smallest airport on this list, LGA ranks 6th for delay rate because of this structural constraint.

# Passenger Boarding (Enplanement) and All-Cargo Data for U.S. Airports

Passenger boarding (enplanement) and all-cargo data is extracted from the FAA's Air Carrier Activity database. This database supports the FAA's airport categories for use in apportionment formula calculations under the [Airport Improvement Program (AIP)](https://www.faa.gov/airports/aip) and [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act programs](https://www.faa.gov/iija).  
[More about the collection and use of passenger and all-cargo data »](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/passenger/collection)

Passenger boarding and all-cargo data is collected for a full calendar year and is used in calculating airport categories and entitlements for the next full fiscal year (i.e., Calendar Year 2025 data determines Fiscal Year 2027 category and funds).

*   **Preliminary**Calendar Year 2025 enplanement and all-cargo data will be available in June 2026.
    *   Any major discrepancies or have questions concerning preliminary all-cargo data or enplanements should promptly be directed to Mr. Luis Loarte at [Luis.Loarte@faa.gov](mailto:Luis.Loarte@faa.gov?subject=Question%20about%20all-cargo%20data%20and%20enplanements) or Mrs. Christina Nutting at [Christina.Nutting@faa.gov](mailto:Christina.Nutting@faa.gov?subject=Question%20about%20all-cargo%20data%20and%20enplanements) by August 14, 2026.

*   **Final**Calendar Year 2025 enplanement and all-cargo data will become available in late August 2026.

Airports can view their individual CY 2025 enplanement report on our [Airports External Portal (AEP)](https://aep.airports.faa.gov/Home.aspx). Please select "Enplanement Public Report and Form" on the AEP site.

See Abbreviations for an explanation of the abbreviations used in the enplanements and cargo files column headings.

## Abbreviations

*   CY = Calendar Year (January 1 through December 31)
*   RO = [FAA Regional Office](https://www.faa.gov/about/office_org/headquarters_offices/arp/offices/regional_offices)
*   ST = Abbreviation for U.S. State or Territory
*   Locid = Location Identifier for a specific airport
*   S/L = Service Level - These are [Airport Categories](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/categories) (P = Primary, CS = Commercial Service, GA = General Aviation).
*   Hub = Hub Size and applies to Commercial Service [Airport Categories](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/categories) (L = Large, M = Medium, S = Small, N = Nonhub Primary, and None = All airports but Primary) based on total CY enplanements.

# Passenger Boarding (Enplanement) and All-Cargo Data for U.S. Airports

Passenger boarding (enplanement) and all-cargo data is extracted from the FAA's Air Carrier Activity database. This database supports the FAA's airport categories for use in apportionment formula calculations under the [Airport Improvement Program (AIP)](https://www.faa.gov/airports/aip) and [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act programs](https://www.faa.gov/iija).  
[More about the collection and use of passenger and all-cargo data »](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/passenger/collection)

Passenger boarding and all-cargo data is collected for a full calendar year and is used in calculating airport categories and entitlements for the next full fiscal year (i.e., Calendar Year 2025 data determines Fiscal Year 2027 category and funds).

*   **Preliminary**Calendar Year 2025 enplanement and all-cargo data will be available in June 2026.
    *   Any major discrepancies or have questions concerning preliminary all-cargo data or enplanements should promptly be directed to Mr. Luis Loarte at [Luis.Loarte@faa.gov](mailto:Luis.Loarte@faa.gov?subject=Question%20about%20all-cargo%20data%20and%20enplanements) or Mrs. Christina Nutting at [Christina.Nutting@faa.gov](mailto:Christina.Nutting@faa.gov?subject=Question%20about%20all-cargo%20data%20and%20enplanements) by August 14, 2026.

*   **Final**Calendar Year 2025 enplanement and all-cargo data will become available in late August 2026.

Airports can view their individual CY 2025 enplanement report on our [Airports External Portal (AEP)](https://aep.airports.faa.gov/Home.aspx). Please select "Enplanement Public Report and Form" on the AEP site.

See Abbreviations for an explanation of the abbreviations used in the enplanements and cargo files column headings.

# U.S. International Air Passenger and Freight Statistics Report

## **Overview**

The U.S. International Air Passenger and Freight Statistics report has been developed to provide the public with additional access to international aviation data. The report is restricted to commercial traffic that travels on nonstop segments between international points and the United States. The data includes totals for departures, passengers, seats, and freight.

## **Technical Notes**

This report represents a limited aspect of international travel - nonstop segment flows into and out of the United States . These airports serve as international gateways and will have high numbers in this report, but users should understand that some portion of this traffic continued on a connecting flight to their final destination. For example, U.S. carriers serve some international points only through an international connection; therefore it might appear as if no U.S. carrier serves a certain international point when in fact U.S. carrier traffic is first flowing through a connecting city. Figures for U.S. nonstop market share do not necessarily correlate to the total service provided to that point by all U.S. carriers.

The widespread use of code-share agreements between U.S. and foreign carriers also influences this data. Under a code-share agreement, it is common for a passenger to fly on an aircraft owned and operated by a different airline than the one from which they bought their ticket. The data in this report represents the air carrier that operated the passenger or cargo flight reported. In some cases, regulatory impediments make it difficult for U.S. carriers to operate adequate international service using their own equipment. U.S. carriers compensate by marketing and selling tickets under their own code to those destinations while the foreign code-share partner is responsible for operating the flight and providing transport. Therefore, low U.S. market share in certain restricted markets is not indicative of the true proportion of passengers purchasing tickets from U.S. carriers. Code-sharing and network- flow data issues also apply to cargo shipments.

The data in this report is presented in a top-down format. Table 1 provides gross summaries of U.S.-International passengers, capacity, and freight. The same data is then broken down by world area and by country in Tables 2 through 5. Scheduled passenger data for the largest domestic gateway cities, the largest foreign gateway cities, and the largest U.S.- International city-pairs can be found in Tables 6 through 8. All data is derived from the T-100 Segment reports submitted to the Department by U.S. and foreign carriers.

## **About the T-100 Program**

The T-100 program was instituted by the Department of Transportation effective January 1, 1990. It covers traffic reports of foreign airlines operating to and from the United States and traffic reports of the domestic and international operations of U.S. airlines. The airlines submit these reports monthly to the Department’s Office of Airline Information (OAI) of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. The rules governing disclosure of the International T-100 data provide that data be kept confidential for a period of six months beyond the reporting date.

Users of this report should take the following points into consideration:

*   The T-100 segment data includes all traffic arriving at U.S. airports and departing from U.S. airports on nonstop commercial international flights.
*   T-100 segment data represents only nonstop service. The absence of U.S. nonstop service, or a low U.S. flag market share, does not necessarily correlate to the amount of service provided to that point by U.S. carriers. Many international destinations are served by U.S. carriers via connecting points.
*   Traffic on U.S.– International routes that serve as connecting gateways will likely exceed the number of true Origin & Destination passengers in the market because of a significant percentage of traffic connecting through the gateway to other markets.
*   T-100 data is reported according to the operating carrier.Code-share relationships may cause U.S. carriers to seem under-represented in certain restrictive markets. In extensive code-share relationships, U.S. airlines sell a large number of tickets to passengers with transport provided by the foreign code-share partner.
*   Cargo carriers also employ the use of interline and connecting networks; therefore, cargo data is susceptible to the same reporting shortcomings in this report as passenger data.
*   Freight tons do not include mail.

# U.S. International Air Passenger and Freight Statistics Report

## **Overview**

The U.S. International Air Passenger and Freight Statistics report has been developed to provide the public with additional access to international aviation data. The report is restricted to commercial traffic that travels on nonstop segments between international points and the United States. The data includes totals for departures, passengers, seats, and freight.

## **Technical Notes**

This report represents a limited aspect of international travel - nonstop segment flows into and out of the United States . These airports serve as international gateways and will have high numbers in this report, but users should understand that some portion of this traffic continued on a connecting flight to their final destination. For example, U.S. carriers serve some international points only through an international connection; therefore it might appear as if no U.S. carrier serves a certain international point when in fact U.S. carrier traffic is first flowing through a connecting city. Figures for U.S. nonstop market share do not necessarily correlate to the total service provided to that point by all U.S. carriers.

The widespread use of code-share agreements between U.S. and foreign carriers also influences this data. Under a code-share agreement, it is common for a passenger to fly on an aircraft owned and operated by a different airline than the one from which they bought their ticket. The data in this report represents the air carrier that operated the passenger or cargo flight reported. In some cases, regulatory impediments make it difficult for U.S. carriers to operate adequate international service using their own equipment. U.S. carriers compensate by marketing and selling tickets under their own code to those destinations while the foreign code-share partner is responsible for operating the flight and providing transport. Therefore, low U.S. market share in certain restricted markets is not indicative of the true proportion of passengers purchasing tickets from U.S. carriers. Code-sharing and network- flow data issues also apply to cargo shipments.

The data in this report is presented in a top-down format. Table 1 provides gross summaries of U.S.-International passengers, capacity, and freight. The same data is then broken down by world area and by country in Tables 2 through 5. Scheduled passenger data for the largest domestic gateway cities, the largest foreign gateway cities, and the largest U.S.- International city-pairs can be found in Tables 6 through 8. All data is derived from the T-100 Segment reports submitted to the Department by U.S. and foreign carriers.

## **About the T-100 Program**

The T-100 program was instituted by the Department of Transportation effective January 1, 1990. It covers traffic reports of foreign airlines operating to and from the United States and traffic reports of the domestic and international operations of U.S. airlines. The airlines submit these reports monthly to the Department’s Office of Airline Information (OAI) of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. The rules governing disclosure of the International T-100 data provide that data be kept confidential for a period of six months beyond the reporting date.

Users of this report should take the following points into consideration:

*   The T-100 segment data includes all traffic arriving at U.S. airports and departing from U.S. airports on nonstop commercial international flights.
*   T-100 segment data represents only nonstop service. The absence of U.S. nonstop service, or a low U.S. flag market share, does not necessarily correlate to the amount of service provided to that point by U.S. carriers. Many international destinations are served by U.S. carriers via connecting points.
*   Traffic on U.S.– International routes that serve as connecting gateways will likely exceed the number of true Origin & Destination passengers in the market because of a significant percentage of traffic connecting through the gateway to other markets.
*   T-100 data is reported according to the operating carrier.Code-share relationships may cause U.S. carriers to seem under-represented in certain restrictive markets. In extensive code-share relationships, U.S. airlines sell a large number of tickets to passengers with transport provided by the foreign code-share partner.
*   Cargo carriers also employ the use of interline and connecting networks; therefore, cargo data is susceptible to the same reporting shortcomings in this report as passenger data.
*   Freight tons do not include mail.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

For consistency, the [Airports Council International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Council_International "Airports Council International")'s (ACI) annual figures are always used in the final presentation and ranking, even where figures given by airport operators or authorities differ.

This article is about the busiest airports by passenger traffic. For the busiest airports in the world by international passenger traffic, see [List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic"). For the busiest cities by passenger traffic, see [List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_(cropped).jpg)

[Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") in the [Atlanta metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta"), the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic as of 2025

The world's busiest airport is [Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") in [metropolitan Atlanta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta"), which has been the world's busiest airport every year since 1998 with the exception of 2020, when its passenger traffic dipped for a year due to travel restrictions resulting from the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_commercial_air_transport "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on commercial air transport").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-1) Atlanta regained the top position in 2021,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-PANYNJ_2021_report-3) and has held it since. Alternatively, London has the [world's busiest city airport system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic") by passenger count.

As of 2025, the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") has the most airports in the top 50 list, with 14 (15 in 2024), followed by [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") with 12 (same as in 2024), while [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") each have two. In terms of regions, [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") has 15 airports in the top 50 (17 in 2024), along with [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") also with 15 (14 in 2024), [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") with eight (same as in 2024), [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") with five (same as in 2024), [West Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Asia "West Asia") with four (three in 2024), [South Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") with two (same as 2024), and [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America") with one (same as 2024).

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

For consistency, the [Airports Council International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Council_International "Airports Council International")'s (ACI) annual figures are always used in the final presentation and ranking, even where figures given by airport operators or authorities differ.

This article is about the busiest airports by passenger traffic. For the busiest airports in the world by international passenger traffic, see [List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic"). For the busiest cities by passenger traffic, see [List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_(cropped).jpg)

[Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") in the [Atlanta metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta"), the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic as of 2025

The world's busiest airport is [Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") in [metropolitan Atlanta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta"), which has been the world's busiest airport every year since 1998 with the exception of 2020, when its passenger traffic dipped for a year due to travel restrictions resulting from the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_commercial_air_transport "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on commercial air transport").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-1) Atlanta regained the top position in 2021,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-PANYNJ_2021_report-3) and has held it since. Alternatively, London has the [world's busiest city airport system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic") by passenger count.

As of 2025, the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") has the most airports in the top 50 list, with 14 (15 in 2024), followed by [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") with 12 (same as in 2024), while [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") each have two. In terms of regions, [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") has 15 airports in the top 50 (17 in 2024), along with [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") also with 15 (14 in 2024), [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") with eight (same as in 2024), [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") with five (same as in 2024), [West Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Asia "West Asia") with four (three in 2024), [South Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") with two (same as 2024), and [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America") with one (same as 2024).

#### What is OTP

On-time performance (OTP) data is critical to understanding the performance of airlines and airports.

Across the aviation industry, an airline departure or arrival occurring****within 15 minutes****of the scheduled time is considered on-time.[](https://www.oag.com/on-time-performance-airlines-airports)

OTP is a crucial key performance indicator for airlines and airports, it helps to gauge their efficiency and also has the potential to set them apart from their competitors.

#### Understanding the data

On-time performance data shows the percentage of flights that have**departed (for airports)**or**arrived (for airlines)**on-time.

A flight is considered on-time if it has departed or arrived**within 15 minutes**of the schedule.

The higher the percentage, the better the OTP score.

**Cancellations**are included in our data and are considered**not**on-time.

For an airline or airport's OTP to be published, OAG requires access to flight status data for at least**80% of all scheduled flights operated,**and**to be ranked they must operate a minimum of 1,500 flights**that month.

**Not included? Contact us and we will be happy to discuss our requirements.**

[Get in touch](https://www.oag.com/airline-partner-hub)

## Frequently asked questions

*   How is airport OTP calculatedAirport on-time performance is based on actual gate departure times. Flights that depart within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Departing 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered not on-time.  
*   How is airline OTP calculated?**Airline**on-time performance is based on**actual gate****arrival times**. Flights that arrive within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Arriving 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered**not on-time**.  
*   Why is OTP important?OTP is valuable for operations management; delays affect productivity and lead to increased costs. Flight punctuality is also of the highest importance to the traveler, poor punctuality will mean that flights arrive at their gate late or depart late – which could lead to passengers missing connecting flights.   
*   Which airports are included?Airports included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 departures in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Which airlines are included?Airlines included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 scheduled flights in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Why is my airline/airport not included?To be included in OAG's rankings airlines and airports must reach a minimum size criteria and a coverage qualification. To discuss our requirements in more detail, click the link below.  
*   How often is the data refreshed?The OTP data is updated each month, usually during the second week. You can sign up to receive notifications by clicking on the link below.

# 357+ US Airport Codes Categorized For Ease Of Use [Updated 2026]

If you are looking for US Airport codes you have come to the right place. This comprehensive guide features a United States airport codes list organized in multiple ways to help you quickly find the airport you need. We have also categorized the codes by airport size. If you are looking for the major US airport hub codes, you’ll find them there.

Airport codes are the standardized three-letter identifiers assigned by the International Air Transport Association (IATA). These letter codes make it easier for airlines, airports, travel agencies, and passengers to identify airports accurately when booking flights, tracking baggage, and planning travel. While many travelers refer to them as US airport call letters, these identifiers are officially recognized airport codes used throughout the aviation industry.

Knowing the correct letter codes can simplify booking charter flights, coordinating private aviation itineraries, and understanding airline schedules. # A Key to Deciphering Airport Codes

There's no easy way to understand all of the various airport codes, but at least there are some clues.

[Aimee Carrier](https://magazine.northeast.aaa.com/author/aimee-carrier/)November 21, 2025

Today, an average traveler may never need to know an airport code. Your airline, destination and departure time are often all you need to find your gate and flight status. Although, it’s best to know your flight number too.

You may be at least subliminally aware of the three letters that accompany your flight information on your tickets, boarding passes, luggage tags and the airport’s arrival-departure board.

If you’re headed to Boston, it’s no big deal. The code BOS is straightforward. But if you’re going to Chicago, you may need to know whether you’re landing at Midway (MDW) or O’Hare (ORD). If it’s the latter, you might also find yourself wondering: Why ORD?

It’s a question many of us have pondered at some point. Thankfully, we’ve never mistaken the Windy City in March for sunny Orlando, Florida, airport code MCO. Or have we? The codes for O’Hare and Orlando are perhaps the most puzzlingly familiar. But with hundreds of airports across the U.S., each with its own unique code, they’re not alone.

## The Origin of Airport Codes

The codes air passengers most often see are from the International Air Transport Association (IATA), which established the three-letter system for commercial airlines starting in the 1960s. Airports may be assigned different codes by the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://www.faa.gov/) (FAA) and the [International Civil Aviation Organization](https://www.icao.int/) (ICAO). Airports can request specific codes, but they’re not always granted.

There’s no decoder ring, all we can do is follow a few rules and some clues.

## Formerly Known As

Some airports that predate the IATA codes had well-established two-letter codes that were incorporated into their three-letter identifiers. Or an IATA code may correspond to an airport’s previous name. IATA codes are permanent. Just imagine how disruptive changing airport codes could be. Here are some examples.

*   **BNA:** Tennessee’s Nashville International Airport was once Berry Field.
*   **MCO:** Florida’s Orlando International Airport was formerly McCoy Airforce Base. ORL belongs to Orlando Executive Airport.
*   **MSY:** It may seem a mystery, but the code for Louisiana’s Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport is short for Moisant Stock Yards, where it was built.
*   **ORD:** Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport was Orchard Field Airport until 1949, when it was renamed to honor a World War II pilot.
*   **SDF:** Kentucky’s Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport was once Standiford Field, named for the owner of the land where it was built. It was Louisville International Airport from 1995 to 2019, when it was renamed to honor local son and boxing legend Muhammad Ali.

## No N’s Allowed

The U.S. Navy reserves codes beginning with the letter N. K and W are also reserved for U.S. radio call letters. That’s why these airports have peculiar codes.

*   **EWR:** Newark Liberty International Airport, New Jersey.
*   **EYW**: Key West International Airport, Florida
*   **HVN:** Tweed New Haven Airport, Connecticut.
*   **ICT**: Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport, Kansas
*   **ORF:** Norfolk International Airport, Virginia.
*   **OME:** Nome Airport, Alaska.

## Ends With an X

An X at the end of an IATA airport code could be an extension of an existing two-letter code, as in:

*   **LAX:** Los Angeles International Airport, California.
*   **PHX:** Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, Arizona.
*   **PDX:** Portland International Airport, Oregon, not to be confused with Portland International Jetport in Maine (PWM).

But sometimes an X has greater meaning.

*   **JAX:** Unlike other X-ending airports, Florida’s Jacksonville International Airport code reflects the city’s nickname for itself. Jacksonville, North Carolina’s Albert J. Ellis Airport is OAJ. JAC belongs to Jackson Hole Airport in Wyoming.
*   **SUX:** The code for Iowa’s Sioux Gateway Airport may have an unfortunate pronunciation, but the letters do reflect its name. Sioux Falls Regional Airport in South Dakota may have given it a little more thought when it requested FSD, which stands for Falls, Sioux, Dakota.

## All-American

*   **USA:** It’s hard to believe that the country’s most patriotic IATA airport code didn’t come into being until 2013. And it was bestowed on North Carolina’s Concord–Padgett Regional Airport, which has only two airlines with limited flights to Florida and the Northeast. This is also an example of an airport’s IATA code not matching its ICAO code (KJQF) or its FAA code (JQF).

## Top 20

Now that we know a little about airport codes, let’s make a list of those you’re most likely to see. In 2024, these were the 20 [busiest airports](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/passenger/arp-cy2024-commercial-service-enplanements.pdf) by passengers, according to the FAA.

1.   **ATL**: Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Georgia.
2.   **DFW**: Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Texas.
3.   **DEN**: Denver International Airport, Colorado.
4.   **ORD**: O’Hare International Airport, Illinois.
5.   **LAX**: Los Angeles International Airport, California.
6.   **JFK**: John F. Kennedy International Airport, New York.
7.   **CLT**: Charlotte Douglas International Airport, North Carolina.
8.   **LAS**: Harry Reid International Airport, Nevada.
9.   **MCO**: Orlando International Airport, Florida.
10.   **MIA**: Miami International Airport, Florida.
11.   **PHX**: Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, Arizona.
12.   **SEA**: Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, Washington.
13.   **SFO**: San Francisco International Airport, California.
14.   **EWR**: Newark Liberty International Airport, New Jersey.
15.   **IAH**: George Bush Intercontinental Airport, Texas.
16.   **BOS**: Boston Logan International Airport, Massachusetts.
17.   **MSP**: Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport, Minnesota.
18.   **FLL**: Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood International Airport, Florida.
19.   **LGA**: LaGuardia Airport, New York.
20.   **DTW**: Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport, Michigan.

# A Key to Deciphering Airport Codes

There's no easy way to understand all of the various airport codes, but at least there are some clues.

[Aimee Carrier](https://magazine.northeast.aaa.com/author/aimee-carrier/)November 21, 2025

Today, an average traveler may never need to know an airport code. Your airline, destination and departure time are often all you need to find your gate and flight status. Although, it’s best to know your flight number too.

You may be at least subliminally aware of the three letters that accompany your flight information on your tickets, boarding passes, luggage tags and the airport’s arrival-departure board.

If you’re headed to Boston, it’s no big deal. The code BOS is straightforward. But if you’re going to Chicago, you may need to know whether you’re landing at Midway (MDW) or O’Hare (ORD). If it’s the latter, you might also find yourself wondering: Why ORD?

It’s a question many of us have pondered at some point. Thankfully, we’ve never mistaken the Windy City in March for sunny Orlando, Florida, airport code MCO. Or have we? The codes for O’Hare and Orlando are perhaps the most puzzlingly familiar. But with hundreds of airports across the U.S., each with its own unique code, they’re not alone.

## The Origin of Airport Codes

The codes air passengers most often see are from the International Air Transport Association (IATA), which established the three-letter system for commercial airlines starting in the 1960s. Airports may be assigned different codes by the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://www.faa.gov/) (FAA) and the [International Civil Aviation Organization](https://www.icao.int/) (ICAO). Airports can request specific codes, but they’re not always granted.

There’s no decoder ring, all we can do is follow a few rules and some clues.

## Formerly Known As

Some airports that predate the IATA codes had well-established two-letter codes that were incorporated into their three-letter identifiers. Or an IATA code may correspond to an airport’s previous name. IATA codes are permanent. Just imagine how disruptive changing airport codes could be. Here are some examples.

*   **BNA:** Tennessee’s Nashville International Airport was once Berry Field.
*   **MCO:** Florida’s Orlando International Airport was formerly McCoy Airforce Base. ORL belongs to Orlando Executive Airport.
*   **MSY:** It may seem a mystery, but the code for Louisiana’s Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport is short for Moisant Stock Yards, where it was built.
*   **ORD:** Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport was Orchard Field Airport until 1949, when it was renamed to honor a World War II pilot.
*   **SDF:** Kentucky’s Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport was once Standiford Field, named for the owner of the land where it was built. It was Louisville International Airport from 1995 to 2019, when it was renamed to honor local son and boxing legend Muhammad Ali.

## No N’s Allowed

The U.S. Navy reserves codes beginning with the letter N. K and W are also reserved for U.S. radio call letters. That’s why these airports have peculiar codes.

*   **EWR:** Newark Liberty International Airport, New Jersey.
*   **EYW**: Key West International Airport, Florida
*   **HVN:** Tweed New Haven Airport, Connecticut.
*   **ICT**: Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport, Kansas
*   **ORF:** Norfolk International Airport, Virginia.
*   **OME:** Nome Airport, Alaska.

## Ends With an X

An X at the end of an IATA airport code could be an extension of an existing two-letter code, as in:

*   **LAX:** Los Angeles International Airport, California.
*   **PHX:** Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, Arizona.
*   **PDX:** Portland International Airport, Oregon, not to be confused with Portland International Jetport in Maine (PWM).

But sometimes an X has greater meaning.

*   **JAX:** Unlike other X-ending airports, Florida’s Jacksonville International Airport code reflects the city’s nickname for itself. Jacksonville, North Carolina’s Albert J. Ellis Airport is OAJ. JAC belongs to Jackson Hole Airport in Wyoming.
*   **SUX:** The code for Iowa’s Sioux Gateway Airport may have an unfortunate pronunciation, but the letters do reflect its name. Sioux Falls Regional Airport in South Dakota may have given it a little more thought when it requested FSD, which stands for Falls, Sioux, Dakota.

## All-American

*   **USA:** It’s hard to believe that the country’s most patriotic IATA airport code didn’t come into being until 2013. And it was bestowed on North Carolina’s Concord–Padgett Regional Airport, which has only two airlines with limited flights to Florida and the Northeast. This is also an example of an airport’s IATA code not matching its ICAO code (KJQF) or its FAA code (JQF).

## Top 20

Now that we know a little about airport codes, let’s make a list of those you’re most likely to see. In 2024, these were the 20 [busiest airports](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/passenger/arp-cy2024-commercial-service-enplanements.pdf) by passengers, according to the FAA.

1.   **ATL**: Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Georgia.
2.   **DFW**: Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Texas.
3.   **DEN**: Denver International Airport, Colorado.
4.   **ORD**: O’Hare International Airport, Illinois.
5.   **LAX**: Los Angeles International Airport, California.
6.   **JFK**: John F. Kennedy International Airport, New York.
7.   **CLT**: Charlotte Douglas International Airport, North Carolina.
8.   **LAS**: Harry Reid International Airport, Nevada.
9.   **MCO**: Orlando International Airport, Florida.
10.   **MIA**: Miami International Airport, Florida.
11.   **PHX**: Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, Arizona.
12.   **SEA**: Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, Washington.
13.   **SFO**: San Francisco International Airport, California.
14.   **EWR**: Newark Liberty International Airport, New Jersey.
15.   **IAH**: George Bush Intercontinental Airport, Texas.
16.   **BOS**: Boston Logan International Airport, Massachusetts.
17.   **MSP**: Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport, Minnesota.
18.   **FLL**: Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood International Airport, Florida.
19.   **LGA**: LaGuardia Airport, New York.
20.   **DTW**: Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport, Michigan.

What is an IATA three-letter airport code?

United States airports, as well as airports around the world use a universal unique three-letter airport code, or Location Identifier defined by the International Air Transport Association. It's easier to say, and write LAX than Los Angeles International Airport for the pilots, controllers, travel agents, frequent flyers, computers and baggage handlers. It's the three-letter code you see on baggage tags in the airport.

Are there four-character codes?

The ICAO airport code is a four-character alphanumeric code used to designate all airport around the world as defined by the International Civil Aviation Organization. ICAO codes differ from the IATA codes used for reservations and baggage, as they are used by air traffic control for flight planning and airline operations, and are not included in this list.

What is an IATA three-letter airport code?

United States airports, as well as airports around the world use a universal unique three-letter airport code, or Location Identifier defined by the International Air Transport Association. It's easier to say, and write LAX than Los Angeles International Airport for the pilots, controllers, travel agents, frequent flyers, computers and baggage handlers. It's the three-letter code you see on baggage tags in the airport.

Are there four-character codes?

The ICAO airport code is a four-character alphanumeric code used to designate all airport around the world as defined by the International Civil Aviation Organization. ICAO codes differ from the IATA codes used for reservations and baggage, as they are used by air traffic control for flight planning and airline operations, and are not included in this list.

	using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
	using GeoTimeZone;        // Import from Nuget package "GeoTimeZone"  (https://github.com/mattjohnsonpint/GeoTimeZone)
	using TimeZoneConverter;  // Import from Nuget package "TimeZoneConverter"  (https://github.com/mattjohnsonpint/TimeZoneConverter)
	

	namespace AirportTimeZones;
	

	internal static class Program
	{
	    private static void Main()
	    {
	        // Get the airports.csv data file from here: http://ourairports.com/data/
	

	        using var reader = File.OpenText("airports.csv");
	        var header = reader.ReadLine();
	        if (header == null)
	            return;
	

	        var csvRegex = new Regex("((?<=\")[^\"]*(?=\"(,|$)+)|(?<=,|^)[^,\"]*(?=,|$))", RegexOptions.Compiled);
	

	        var columns = csvRegex.Matches(header).Select((m, i) => new { m.Value, Index = i }).ToDictionary(x => x.Value, x => x.Index);
	        var typeIndex = columns["type"];
	        var latIndex = columns["latitude_deg"];
	        var lonIndex = columns["longitude_deg"];
	        var codeIndex = columns["iata_code"];
	

	        var results = new Dictionary<string, string>();
	        string[] badCodes = { "", "-", "---", "0" };
	

	        while (reader.ReadLine() is { } line)
	        {
	            var values = csvRegex.Matches(line);
	

	            var type = values[typeIndex].Value;
	            var code = values[codeIndex].Value;
	

	            if (badCodes.Contains(code) || type == "closed" || results.ContainsKey(code))
	                continue;
	

	            var lat = double.Parse(values[latIndex].Value);
	            var lon = double.Parse(values[lonIndex].Value);
	            var tz = TimeZoneLookup.GetTimeZone(lat, lon).Result;
	

	            results.Add(code, tz);
	        }
	

	        using var writer = File.CreateText("timezones.csv");
	        
	        writer.WriteLine("\"iata_code\",\"iana_tz\",\"windows_tz\"");
	        foreach (var item in results.OrderBy(x => x.Key))
	        {
	            if (!TZConvert.TryIanaToWindows(item.Value, out var windowsTimeZone)) 
	                windowsTimeZone = string.Empty;
	            
	            writer.WriteLine("\"{0}\",\"{1}\",\"{2}\"", item.Key, item.Value, windowsTimeZone);
	        }
	    }
	}

	using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
	using GeoTimeZone;        // Import from Nuget package "GeoTimeZone"  (https://github.com/mattjohnsonpint/GeoTimeZone)
	using TimeZoneConverter;  // Import from Nuget package "TimeZoneConverter"  (https://github.com/mattjohnsonpint/TimeZoneConverter)
	

	namespace AirportTimeZones;
	

	internal static class Program
	{
	    private static void Main()
	    {
	        // Get the airports.csv data file from here: http://ourairports.com/data/
	

	        using var reader = File.OpenText("airports.csv");
	        var header = reader.ReadLine();
	        if (header == null)
	            return;
	

	        var csvRegex = new Regex("((?<=\")[^\"]*(?=\"(,|$)+)|(?<=,|^)[^,\"]*(?=,|$))", RegexOptions.Compiled);
	

	        var columns = csvRegex.Matches(header).Select((m, i) => new { m.Value, Index = i }).ToDictionary(x => x.Value, x => x.Index);
	        var typeIndex = columns["type"];
	        var latIndex = columns["latitude_deg"];
	        var lonIndex = columns["longitude_deg"];
	        var codeIndex = columns["iata_code"];
	

	        var results = new Dictionary<string, string>();
	        string[] badCodes = { "", "-", "---", "0" };
	

	        while (reader.ReadLine() is { } line)
	        {
	            var values = csvRegex.Matches(line);
	

	            var type = values[typeIndex].Value;
	            var code = values[codeIndex].Value;
	

	            if (badCodes.Contains(code) || type == "closed" || results.ContainsKey(code))
	                continue;
	

	            var lat = double.Parse(values[latIndex].Value);
	            var lon = double.Parse(values[lonIndex].Value);
	            var tz = TimeZoneLookup.GetTimeZone(lat, lon).Result;
	

	            results.Add(code, tz);
	        }
	

	        using var writer = File.CreateText("timezones.csv");
	        
	        writer.WriteLine("\"iata_code\",\"iana_tz\",\"windows_tz\"");
	        foreach (var item in results.OrderBy(x => x.Key))
	        {
	            if (!TZConvert.TryIanaToWindows(item.Value, out var windowsTimeZone)) 
	                windowsTimeZone = string.Empty;
	            
	            writer.WriteLine("\"{0}\",\"{1}\",\"{2}\"", item.Key, item.Value, windowsTimeZone);
	        }
	    }
	}

The DST column shows the months in which Daylight Saving Time, a.k.a. Summer Time, begins and ends. A blank DST box usually indicates that the location stays on Standard Time all year, although in some cases the location stays on Summer Time all year. If a location is currently on DST, add one hour to the time in the Time column.

**WASHINGTON —**
About 6 million U.S. travelers are expected to fly domestically this Thanksgiving holiday, with Orlando, San Francisco and Honolulu among the top destinations, according to [AAA](https://newsroom.aaa.com/2025/11/aaa-thanksgiving-travel-forecast-2025/).

Travelers heading to Honolulu are in luck, Daniel K. Inouye International Airport had the best on-time performance in 2025 among the top 50 U.S. airports by passenger traffic, according to the [Bureau of Transportation Statistics](https://www.transtats.bts.gov/airports.asp).

Advertisement

Honolulu's airport saw 87% of arrivals and 88% of departures leave on time from August 2024 to July 2025. That is based on the most recent data BTS provides for domestic flights and labels the period as 2025 data. From this time period, Daniel K. Inouye had a total of 25,300 flights.

Salt Lake City International, St. Louis Lambert International and John Wayne Airport-Orange County had the next highest on-time arrival rates, each at 85%. Among the three, Salt Lake City had the most domestic flights with 115,000, while St. Louis Lambert and John Wayne had a combined 45,800.

The lowest on-time arrival rates were at Ronald Reagan Washington National and Newark Liberty International, with both at 72%. Between August 2024 and July 2025, Reagan operated 141,800 flights and Newark operated 122,600. Philadelphia International had the second-lowest on-time arrival rate at 74% with 99,600 flights.

Three airports were behind Honolulu for on-time departures: Portland International, Kansas City International and Indianapolis International. All had an on-time departure rate of 86%.

Dallas-Fort Worth International had the lowest on-time departure rate of 71% with 318,100 flights.

Baltimore Washington International Thurgood Marshall had a slightly higher on-time departure rate of 73%, but far fewer flights — 97,000 compared to Dallas-Fort Worth.

Still, Dallas-Fort Worth was not the busiest airport in the country. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International had 326,600 flights, with an on-time departure rate of 77% and 81% for arrivals.

Honolulu's airport saw 87% of arrivals and 88% of departures leave on time from August 2024 to July 2025. That is based on the most recent data BTS provides for domestic flights and labels the period as 2025 data. From this time period, Daniel K. Inouye had a total of 25,300 flights.

Salt Lake City International, St. Louis Lambert International and John Wayne Airport-Orange County had the next highest on-time arrival rates, each at 85%. Among the three, Salt Lake City had the most domestic flights with 115,000, while St. Louis Lambert and John Wayne had a combined 45,800.

The lowest on-time arrival rates were at Ronald Reagan Washington National and Newark Liberty International, with both at 72%. Between August 2024 and July 2025, Reagan operated 141,800 flights and Newark operated 122,600. Philadelphia International had the second-lowest on-time arrival rate at 74% with 99,600 flights.

Three airports were behind Honolulu for on-time departures: Portland International, Kansas City International and Indianapolis International. All had an on-time departure rate of 86%.

Dallas-Fort Worth International had the lowest on-time departure rate of 71% with 318,100 flights.

Baltimore Washington International Thurgood Marshall had a slightly higher on-time departure rate of 73%, but far fewer flights — 97,000 compared to Dallas-Fort Worth.

Still, Dallas-Fort Worth was not the busiest airport in the country. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International had 326,600 flights, with an on-time departure rate of 77% and 81% for arrivals.

#### What is OTP

On-time performance (OTP) data is critical to understanding the performance of airlines and airports.

Across the aviation industry, an airline departure or arrival occurring****within 15 minutes****of the scheduled time is considered on-time.[](https://www.oag.com/on-time-performance-airlines-airports)

OTP is a crucial key performance indicator for airlines and airports, it helps to gauge their efficiency and also has the potential to set them apart from their competitors.

#### Understanding the data

On-time performance data shows the percentage of flights that have**departed (for airports)**or**arrived (for airlines)**on-time.

A flight is considered on-time if it has departed or arrived**within 15 minutes**of the schedule.

The higher the percentage, the better the OTP score.

**Cancellations**are included in our data and are considered**not**on-time.

For an airline or airport's OTP to be published, OAG requires access to flight status data for at least**80% of all scheduled flights operated,**and**to be ranked they must operate a minimum of 1,500 flights**that month.

**Not included? Contact us and we will be happy to discuss our requirements.**

## Frequently asked questions

*   How is airport OTP calculatedAirport on-time performance is based on actual gate departure times. Flights that depart within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Departing 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered not on-time.  
*   How is airline OTP calculated?**Airline**on-time performance is based on**actual gate****arrival times**. Flights that arrive within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Arriving 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered**not on-time**.  
*   Why is OTP important?OTP is valuable for operations management; delays affect productivity and lead to increased costs. Flight punctuality is also of the highest importance to the traveler, poor punctuality will mean that flights arrive at their gate late or depart late – which could lead to passengers missing connecting flights.   
*   Which airports are included?Airports included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 departures in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Which airlines are included?Airlines included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 scheduled flights in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Why is my airline/airport not included?To be included in OAG's rankings airlines and airports must reach a minimum size criteria and a coverage qualification. To discuss our requirements in more detail, click the link below.  
*   How often is the data refreshed?The OTP data is updated each month, usually during the second week. You can sign up to receive notifications by clicking on the link below.

#### What is OTP

On-time performance (OTP) data is critical to understanding the performance of airlines and airports.

Across the aviation industry, an airline departure or arrival occurring****within 15 minutes****of the scheduled time is considered on-time.[](https://www.oag.com/on-time-performance-airlines-airports)

OTP is a crucial key performance indicator for airlines and airports, it helps to gauge their efficiency and also has the potential to set them apart from their competitors.

#### Understanding the data

On-time performance data shows the percentage of flights that have**departed (for airports)**or**arrived (for airlines)**on-time.

A flight is considered on-time if it has departed or arrived**within 15 minutes**of the schedule.

The higher the percentage, the better the OTP score.

**Cancellations**are included in our data and are considered**not**on-time.

For an airline or airport's OTP to be published, OAG requires access to flight status data for at least**80% of all scheduled flights operated,**and**to be ranked they must operate a minimum of 1,500 flights**that month.

**Not included? Contact us and we will be happy to discuss our requirements.**

[Get in touch](https://www.oag.com/airline-partner-hub)

## Frequently asked questions

*   How is airport OTP calculatedAirport on-time performance is based on actual gate departure times. Flights that depart within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Departing 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered not on-time.  
*   How is airline OTP calculated?**Airline**on-time performance is based on**actual gate****arrival times**. Flights that arrive within 15 minutes of the schedule are considered on-time. Arriving 15 minutes or more after the scheduled time is considered**not on-time**.  
*   Why is OTP important?OTP is valuable for operations management; delays affect productivity and lead to increased costs. Flight punctuality is also of the highest importance to the traveler, poor punctuality will mean that flights arrive at their gate late or depart late – which could lead to passengers missing connecting flights.   
*   Which airports are included?Airports included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 departures in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Which airlines are included?Airlines included in the NAM OTP tables must meet a minimum threshold of at least 1500 scheduled flights in the current month and meet a coverage criteria of 80%.  
*   Why is my airline/airport not included?To be included in OAG's rankings airlines and airports must reach a minimum size criteria and a coverage qualification. To discuss our requirements in more detail, click the link below.  
*   How often is the data refreshed?The OTP data is updated each month, usually during the second week. You can sign up to receive notifications by clicking on the link below.
